# Bitview Studio

Charts of Bitcoin's on-chain data from bitview.space, drawn in the browser (with JavaScript on).

## In short
- A chart is a link: https://bitview.space/studio/#chart= followed by its JSON (below), such as {"layers": [{"series": "price"}, {"series": "realized_price"}]}.
- Its picture alone: the same link with #image= in place of #chart=, a page that is, once drawn, that picture (with only screenshots to work with, take one of it).
- Thousands of ready-made charts (presets), each at an address of its own: https://bitview.space/studio/presets/ and its place, such as https://bitview.space/studio/presets/valuation/mvrv; their sections at the same, ending in a slash, such as https://bitview.space/studio/presets/valuation/; every one listed in https://bitview.space/studio/sitemap.xml.
- From a script in the page: await studio.open(chart); await studio.ready(); await studio.png({ width: 1200, height: 760, scale: 2 }), its picture as a PNG data URL, in one result (see "From a script").

## Opening a chart from a link

A link carries a whole chart: https://bitview.space/studio/#chart= followed by the chart as JSON, URL-encoded or as it is. It opens as a preview: whoever opens it sees the chart, and keeps it or not. All a chart can be is written this way. For example (before encoding):

```js
{"title": "Price and realized price", "range": "4y", "layers": [{"series": "price"}, {"series": "realized_price", "color": "orange"}, {"formula": "A / B", "pane": 2}]}
```

## A chart
- "layers" (the one thing needed): its layers, in order (see below).
- "title".
- "index": its interval: minute10, minute30, hour1, hour4, hour12, day1, day3, week1, month1, month3, month6, year1 or year10 (day1 if none).
- "range": what it shows: 3m, 1y, 4y, 8y or max (8y if none; max: all of history at day1 or coarser; at a finer interval, as far back as fits on the screen). Or "view": {"from": "2021-01-01", "to": "2022-06-30"}, a window by dates: from the bar holding its "from" to the one holding its "to" (now if none). Dates and times are UTC: "2026-10-08", or with a time where it needs one, "2026-10-08T14:00:00Z".
- "panes": [{"mode": 1}, {"mode": 0, "stack": "stack"}], top to bottom: "mode" is its scale (0 linear, 1 logarithmic, 2 percent change, 3 indexed to 100), "stack" stacks its layers ("stack", or "percent" for shares), "size" is its height relative to the others' (3 for the first, 1.4 for the others if none: 1 and 1 halves the chart), "reverse": true puts its last layer in front. Without them, the first pane is logarithmic and the others linear.
- "halvings": true: a line at each halving, and at the next three, estimated (a block each ten minutes).
- "legend": "off": no legend over the panes.
- "drawings" (see below).

## A layer

One of:
- {"series": "realized_price"}: a series, by its exact name.
- {"formula": "A / B"}: computed from other layers by their letters (the first layer is A, the second B, and so on) or from series by name, with + - * / ^, parentheses and functions such as sma(A, 200d), ema, highest, lowest, change, log, percentile(A, 95, 1y), rsi(A), macd(A), volatility(A, 30d), zscore(A) and cagr(A, 4y). when(A, condition) keeps A where the condition holds, none elsewhere; rebase(A) starts each of its stretches at 1×, and rebase(A, halving_epoch) each halving cycle (a stretch also starts where its second changes); halving(A, n) is A over halving cycle n alone from 1× (0 the first, from the genesis block), and halving(A, 0, 2) that cycle moved to start where cycle 2 starts, day for day. date is each point's date, compared with one written 2020-05-11: when(A, date >= 2020-05-11 & date < 2024-04-20); == and != compare too. Spans are a number and a unit: h, d, w, mo or y; some have a usual one if left out, in points as the interval counts them (rsi's 14: 14 days at day1, 14 weeks at week1).
- {"formula": "B > 3.5", "type": "signal", "ref": "A"}: a signal: marks on layer A (the first layer if none) where the formula turns up or down: above 0 is up, below 0 down, 0 off (> < >= <= are 1 or 0, joined with & and |: a condition is up where true; (B > 3.5) - (B < 1) is up, down or off). "place", "below" or "on" (above if none): where an up mark goes, a down one mirrored (above and below swapped), in "colorBelow" (red if none); or "shade": its stretches shaded, its layer's pane's height, down ones in "colorBelow". "results": true: on each mark that ends a stretch, what it made by layer A (A's change over it, up; the opposite, down), a dot where one ends off; their total, compounded, in its line.
- {"cloud": ["B", "C"]}: filled between those layers, two or more, at each date, in the color of the one over: B's own where B is over C, C's where C is (following them). Between more, {"cloud": ["B", "C", "D"]}, a cloud between each two next to each other in that order (B and C, C and D), each in the color of whichever of its two is over: several clouds, made by one (where they cross out of order, two overlap). "color" alone, that one all along, from the lowest to the highest; between two alone, "color" and "colorBelow", those two (where B is over, where C is). "top" and "bottom" are its pane's edges: from its first layer up to the pane's top, from its last down to its bottom: {"cloud": ["A", "top"]}.
- {"trend": ["B", "C"], "ref": "A"}: a line on the lowest of those layers until layer A (a price, say) touches it, then on the highest until A touches that, and so on (A an OHLC series, its highs and lows count, drawn as candles or not; else its value); width and dash as a line's.

Then, each if wanted:
- "label": its name.
- "color": one of Bitview's (gray, red, orange, amber, yellow, avocado, lime, green, emerald, teal, cyan, sky, blue, indigo, violet, purple, fuchsia, pink, rose, or ink, the page's text color) a six-digit hex such as #ff8800, or oklch as Studio writes it, "oklch(0.7 0.15 45)", each as the dark theme (the default) shows it: the light one turns every color's lightness over, white showing as black; "colorBelow": a baseline's or bars' second color, under their base, a trend's on support, or a cloud's where its second layer is over (its own color if none).
- "colorFrom": "B" on a line, dots, an area, bars, a cloud or a trend: its colors taken from layer B date by date, as B is drawn (a baseline's above or below its base, bars' too, a trend's on resistance or support, by its levels if it's colored by them, else B's one color).
- "byLevels": true on a line, dots, an area or bars with levels: colored by them, date by date: above each level, that level's color (give each one its "color"); under them all, its own.
- "colors": 1 or 4 on bars: their one color; or four: above and below their base, each side's own where a bar grows from it ("color", "colorBelow"), fainter where it fades back toward it ("colorFading" above, "colorBelowFading" below; each side's own, fainter, if none). Unset, their two: "color" above, "colorBelow" under. 1 on a trend or a cloud with a "colorBelow": its one color, that second kept.
- "type": line, dots, area, histogram (bars), baseline, or candles (for an OHLC series such as price_ohlc); left out, the series' own look.
- "width": 0.5 to 5, by halves (1.5 if none); "dash": its line (0 solid, 1 dotted, 2 dashed, 3 long dashes, 4 sparse dots); "shape": straight, steps or curved; "opacity": 0.1 to 1, by tenths (1 if none; a cloud's 0.2, solid at 1).
- "hollow": candles' hollow bodies, "down" (falling ones), "both" or "none" (rising ones if none); candles' "colors": 1, their one color (rising in "color", falling in "colorBelow", red if none, unset);
- "fill": "above", an area filled from its line up; "fillOpacity": its fill's strength at its top, 0.05 to 1 (0.2 if none, 0.1 filled above); "solid": true, its fill even all the way down rather than fading; "base": a baseline's or bars' base value (0 if none); "baseLine": {"color": "gray", "dash": 4}, that base's line ("tag": true shows its value on the axis; "line": false draws none).
- "levels": [{"value": 1, "color": "gray", "dash": 3}]: lines across, at values (color and dash optional; "tag": true shows its value on the axis; "line": false draws none, the level only naming or coloring its band). A level's "name" names the values from it up to the next level, read in its color in place of the number (the legend, the panel); "underName" on the layer names those under them all: {"levels": [{"value": -1, "name": "Limbo", "color": "orange", "line": false}, {"value": 1, "name": "Bull", "color": "green", "line": false}], "underName": "Bear", "color": "red", "byLevels": true} (without "byLevels", the names alone, the line in its color).
- "priceLine": true: a line across at its latest value.
- "format": how its values read (by its unit if none): usd, btc, sats, percent, ratio, count, number, days, seconds, persecond, perday, bytes, vbytes, weight, sigops, hashrate, difficulty, feerate, hashprice, hashvalue, coindays, coinblocks, dollarblocks or dollardays.
- "pane": 1, 2 and so on, top to bottom (1 if none); "side": its axis, left or right; "hidden": true.
- "letter": the letter formulas read it by. Copy link writes every layer's once one isn't the letter its place gives (a layer removed leaves the others' as they were): keep them.

## Drawings

"drawings": [{"kind": "trend", "layer": "A", "points": [["2021-04-14", 64000], ["2021-11-10", 69000]]}]: each on a layer (by its letter, on its scale), its points each a date and a value. Kinds: trend (a line through two points), path (a line through two points or more, in their order, up to 300), hline and vline (a line across, or down, through one point: an hline's date and a vline's value can be any), rect and ellipse (by two corners), ruler (a measure between two points), text (at one point, with its "text": up to 500 characters, centered there, "\n" for a new line) and brush (a free stroke, up to 300 points). Up to 100 drawings.

Each can have a "color" (yellow if none), "width" (0.5 to 5, by halves; 1.5 if none), "dash" and "opacity", as a layer's; a ruler is drawn in its own colors and lines (no opacity, width or dash), a text without width or dash. A trend line or a path can have a "start" and an "end" (its first point's and its last's): "arrow", an arrowhead there, or "extend", on past that point to the chart's edge (none: it ends at its point). A trend, hline or vline can have a "label" (up to 80 characters) and where along it ("at", 0 to 1: 0.5 for a trend, 1 for an hline, 0 for a vline if none). A text or a line's label can have a "size" (11, 13, 16 or 22) and a "back" (outline, soft, soft-outline or solid).

## As a picture

A chart shown as an image is its picture, not a screenshot of the page. Three ways to it: from a script in the page, await studio.png() (below), at a size of its own; from a link, https://bitview.space/studio/#image= followed by the chart's JSON, a page that is, once the chart is drawn across the whole window, its picture alone (one image, its alt text the chart's title; a click on it, the chart); by hand, Export (in the chart's ... menu, More, in its header), then Open image (the picture alone, in a tab of its own), Download image (PNG), or Copy image (to the clipboard of whoever uses the browser: an embedded browser may not allow it). The picture is the chart with its title, its legends and a footer (its source, interval and dates).

## From a script

For a script run in the page (a browser's console, an assistant driving a browser), window.studio:
- await studio.open(chart): a chart as a link writes it (an object, or its JSON), opened as its link opens it; rejected with why if it can't be read.
- await studio.ready(): once the chart open is drawn whole (its data in, its reveal and fades at their end: a screenshot then shows all of it); rejected with why not (no chart, no layers, still loading after a minute).
- await studio.png(options): its picture, as Export makes it (its title, legends and dates), as a data URL ("data:image/png;base64," and its base64), in one result, the same whatever the window. If your tool says the output was too long and saved it to a file, decode the base64 from that file: that's the picture, no need to retype it. Options, each if wanted: width and height, in CSS pixels (1200 and 760 if none); scale, 1 or 2 (pixels for each, 1 if none); type, "image/png" (if none), "image/webp" or "image/jpeg", with quality, 0.01 to 1 (0.9 if none); part, only if long output gets cut off and nothing is saved: 0, 1 and so on, each call with part 0's options, the picture in parts, each {part, parts, mime, base64}, partSize characters of its base64 (45000 if none: each part, all told, under 50,000); part 0 makes the picture of the chart as it is, the others are from that same picture, however long after: join their base64, "data:" + mime + ";base64," before it. Sizes, at 1200 by 760, for a chart of a few lines: a PNG about 130,000 to 160,000 characters (three or four parts), a WebP about 50,000, a JPEG about 100,000; at scale 2, about 330,000, 130,000 and 270,000.
- studio.chart(): the chart open, as a link writes it.
- await studio.errors(): once it's drawn, its layers that show nothing, and why, as [{"layer": "B", "error": "...", "closest": "..."}]: a series name Bitview doesn't have (with the closest it has), a series it has only by block (with its day's, if it has one), a formula it can't read.
- await studio.search(words, count): series names for those words (count of them, 10 if not given, 1 to 50), the best first, as Studio's search finds them, only those it can chart (by date; by the words of their names and descriptions: "sma 200d", "transaction count"). No browsing needed: the page knows the catalog, and asks bitview.space only for its first seconds, until its own search is up. It answers within a few seconds, the page shown or not, else it's rejected with why.

What a chart can't hold is left out, or at its default, without a word: past 40 layers, left out; an interval or a range it doesn't know, day1 or 8y.

```js
await studio.open({"title": "Cost basis", "layers": [{"series": "price"}, {"series": "realized_price"}]});
await studio.ready();
const picture = await studio.png({ width: 1200, height: 760, scale: 2 });
// One result: "data:image/png;base64,...". Saved to a file by your tool as too long? Decode the base64 from that file.
// Only if long output is cut off and nothing is saved: the same options with part: 0, then part: 1, 2...
// ({ part, parts, mime, base64 } each; at scale 2, a PNG is six to eight).
```

## Changing a chart

A link is the whole chart, not a change to one: to change it, write it again, changed. Letters follow the layers' order, so a layer added last leaves the formulas' letters as they were. A link copied from Studio (its Copy link, its Share) is compressed, as short as a link gets: it opens, but can't be read (as a Share QR code's, "#c=", compressed in capitals and digits). To change a chart shared that way, open it and read it with studio.chart() (the chart as a link writes it, its JSON), then write it again, changed; a link written out, as here, opens the same. A chart's "view", if any, is where it was zoomed and scrolled: keep it, change it, or leave it out to show the chart's "range".

## Series names

Only exact names, as Bitview's API has them now (the names on this page are examples, and can change): one it doesn't have shows as missing, with the closest offered. How to find them is at https://bitview.space/llms.txt, which follows the API as it is. Only series by date can be charted (some are only by block).

An assistant without web access can't look names up: whoever uses it can, or can add Bitview's MCP server to it as a connector (https://mcp.bitview.space/, no sign-in), for the search and the data as tools.
